title: East of the Sun and West of the Moon
description: A Norwegian folk tale collected by Asbjornsen and Moe. A white bear comes to a poor farmhouse in the north and asks for the youngest daughter, and what follows is a long walk to a castle that lies east of the sun and west of the moon.

beats.narration: East of the Sun and West of the Moon. A folk tale from Norway.
beats.title: East of the Sun
beats.subtitle: A folk tale from Norway

beats.narration: There was a farmer in the north with more children than he could feed, and the youngest of them was the one everyone liked best.
One Thursday evening in autumn, something struck the window. When they opened the door there was a white bear standing in the snow.
Give me your youngest daughter, said the bear, and I will make you as rich as you are poor.
The girl said no. Then she thought about the winter coming, and about her father's face, and by the next Thursday she said yes.
She rode on the bear's back through country she had never seen, and the snow went on for days.
At the end of it a mountain opened, and inside was a castle with every room lit and nobody in it.
She had whatever she asked for. She had only to ring a bell and it was there.
And every night, when the candles were out, someone came and lay down beside her in the dark, and was gone before it was light.
She never saw him. She was never allowed a light. That was the one thing asked of her.
But she grew lonely, and she went home to visit, and her mother told her what she must do.
So she carried a candle to bed, and when he was asleep she lit it, and looked at him.
He was the handsomest man she had ever seen. Three drops of tallow fell on his shirt, and he woke.
If you had waited one year, he said, I would have been free. Now I must go and marry a woman with a nose three ells long.
The castle was gone in the morning and she was lying on a bare hillside, and she began to walk.
She asked the East Wind, who did not know the way. She asked the West Wind, and the South Wind, and none of them had been so far.
The North Wind had been there once, and had come back half dead from it. He carried her, low over the water, for a day and a night.
So she came to the castle that lies east of the sun and west of the moon, and she still had the shirt with the tallow on it.
Nobody in that castle could wash the three drops out. Not the bride, not her mother, not any of them.
She washed it once and it came clean, because it was her candle that had made the marks.
They left before the wedding, and took with them everyone in that place who had been kept there, and did not look back at the mountain.
She lost him by needing to see him, and got him back by walking further than anyone thought a person could walk. The story lets her have both.
This tale was collected in Norway by Peter Asbjornsen and Jorgen Moe, who gathered folk stories across the country in the eighteen forties.

title: Momotaro, the Peach Boy
description: One of the best known folk tales of Japan. An old couple find a child inside a peach, and when he is grown he sets out for the island of the oni with a dog, a monkey and a pheasant beside him.

beats.narration: Momotaro, the Peach Boy. A folk tale from Japan.
beats.title: Momotaro
beats.subtitle: A folk tale from Japan

beats.narration: An old man and an old woman lived in a village between the hills. They had no children, and they had stopped speaking of it.
One morning the woman went down to the river to wash, and something came turning down the current towards her.
It was a peach, and it was the size of a melon, and it bumped against her hands as though it had been aimed.
When she set it on the table to cut it open, the peach split by itself, and there was a child inside, sitting up.
They called him Momotaro, which means peach boy, because they were plain people and it was a plain name for what had happened.
He grew quickly and he grew strong, and when he was still young he told them he was going to the island where the oni lived.
The oni had been coming across the water for years, taking what they wanted from the coast villages. Nobody had gone after them.
His mother made him millet dumplings for the road. That was all she could give him, so she gave him a great many.
On the road a dog came out of the grass and asked what he was carrying. Momotaro gave him a dumpling, and the dog came with him.
Then a monkey, on the path through the trees. Then a pheasant, out of the air. Each one asked, and each one was given, and each one stayed.
At the shore they found a boat, and they rowed out towards the smoke on the horizon.
The island had a wall around it and a gate of iron, and behind the gate the oni were feasting.
The pheasant went over the wall and came down on their heads. The monkey went up the gatepost and drew the bolt. The dog went through first.
It was not a long fight. The oni had never had to defend anything, only to take.
Their chief knelt in the courtyard and promised he would not cross the water again.
They brought back what had been taken, and gave it to the villages it came from, and Momotaro went home to the two people who had found him in a peach.
He did not go alone, and that is the part of the story people forget. He went with everyone who asked, and he fed them first.
Momotaro has been told in Japan for centuries, and written down in many versions since the Edo period. Almost every Japanese child knows him.

title: The Fisherman and His Wife
description: An old tale from northern Germany, written down by the Brothers Grimm. A poor fisherman catches a flounder that can grant wishes, and his wife finds that nothing she is given is ever quite enough. The sea answers every wish with worse weather.

beats.narration: The Fisherman and His Wife. A folk tale from northern Germany.
beats.title: The Fisherman and His Wife
beats.subtitle: A folk tale from northern Germany

beats.narration: There was once a fisherman who lived with his wife in a hut by the sea.
The hut leaned into the wind. It had one room, one window, and a floor of packed earth.
Every morning he rowed out and let down his line, and every evening he came back with what the sea had spared him.
One morning the line went tight and stayed tight, and he pulled up a flounder as broad as a shield.
Let me go, said the flounder. I am no fish. I am an enchanted prince, and I will taste of nothing good.
The fisherman had never heard a fish speak, and he did not argue with one. He opened his hands and let it slide back into the green water.
When he told his wife, she set down her bowl and looked at him for a long moment.
You had a wish in your hands, she said, and you gave it back for nothing. Go and ask him for a cottage.
He did not want to go. But he went, and stood at the edge of the water, and called out over it.
Flounder, flounder in the sea. My wife has sent me. She asks a cottage.
The water rose once, quietly, the way water does when something turns beneath it.
Go home, said the flounder. She has it already.
Where the hut had stood there was a cottage, with a hearth and a bed and a garden behind it.
For a fortnight his wife was pleased. Then she stood at the window and looked at the hills beyond the garden.
A cottage is a small thing, she said. Go and ask him for a castle.
The sea had gone the colour of old iron. The fisherman called out over it, and did not like the sound of his own voice.
The castle had a hall you could ride a horse through, and a hundred candles, and servants who did not meet his eye.
By morning his wife had thought of something else.
What is a castle without a crown, she said. Go and ask him to make me king.
The wind had teeth in it now. The waves came in grey and broke black, and the rain went sideways across the rocks.
Still the flounder came, and still the answer was the same. Go home. She has it already.
She was king. Then she was emperor. Then she was more than that, and each time it took her less time to want the next thing.
At last she sent him out in the dark, and told him what she wanted, and he could not say it aloud on the way.
She wishes, he said at last, to command the sun and the moon to rise.
The sea did not rise. It went flat and black and very still, the way a room goes quiet when someone has said too much.
Go home, said the flounder. She is sitting in the hut.
And she was. The castle was gone, and the cottage with it, and the wind came through the window as it always had.
They are sitting there still, as far as anyone knows.
The tale is not really about the fish. It is about a man who kept walking down to the water because it was easier than saying no.
This story was collected in the nineteenth century by Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, who heard it in the dialect of the Baltic coast.
